steps.title: Four imaginary situations.
steps.sub: None of them is real. Look at the tense in each half.

items.text: If I ran the world, I would build more libraries.
If people didn’t get ill, the hospitals wouldn’t be full.
If we saved half of that food, hunger would be smaller.
What would you do if you had the money?

steps.title: Compare these two sentences.
steps.sub: If it rains, we’ll stay in. · If I ran the world, I would build libraries.
steps.prompt: What is the difference?
options: The first is a real possibility; the second is imaginary or very unlikely.
The first is about the future and the second about the past.
There is no difference.
steps.answer: The first is a real possibility; the second is imaginary or very unlikely.
steps.why: First conditional = it may really happen. Second conditional = imagine it.

steps.title: The second conditional
steps.html:
if + Past Simplewould / wouldn’t + base form
If I ran the world,I would build more libraries.
If people didn’t get ill,the hospitals wouldn’t be full.
If we saved half of that food,hunger would be smaller.
If I were you,I would see a doctor.
What would you doif you had the money?

The Past Simple after if does not mean the past. It shows that the situation is imaginary.

The other half uses would (or wouldn’t) + the base form: I would build, never would to build.

Never put would after if. Say If I had the money, not if I would have.

With be, careful English uses were for every person: If I were you… This is the fixed phrase for giving advice.

You met If I were you, I’d … in Lesson 27 as advice. Now you can see the grammar behind it.

You are going to read five answers to one question.
steps.sub: Which do you think somebody chose? There is no wrong answer here.

steps.title: One change each
steps.sub: Five people, one question, no money.
steps.html:
Reading

We asked five people one question: if you could change one thing about the world, what would it be? Nobody chose money.

Aliya, 23, student. “If I ran the world, I would put every school within walking distance of a library. Not a big one. Twenty books and a room that is warm in winter. If a child had that, half the other problems would get smaller.”

Marat, 47, engineer. “I would spend the money on clean water. It isn’t global warming, it isn’t a natural disaster. It is water. If people didn’t get ill from what they drink, the hospitals wouldn’t be full.”

Dana, 31, doctor. “I would stop food waste before I tried to cure anything. A third of the world’s food is thrown away. If we saved even half of that, hunger would not be an issue in most continents.”

Bekzat, 68, retired teacher. “If every adult spent one hour a week with somebody who has nobody, we would need fewer doctors. It sounds too small to matter. That is why nobody does it.”

Aisha, 15, at school. “I would make the powerful people travel by bus for a month. Then they would understand the problem, and the problem would be fixed by June.”

Five answers, five different worlds. Not one of them is impossible. That is the uncomfortable part.

steps.title: Choose the best answer.
steps.prompt: What does the writer mean by “that is the uncomfortable part”?
options: None of the five changes is impossible — so nothing is stopping us.
All five of the ideas would cost far too much money to do.
The five people disagreed with each other about everything.
steps.answer: None of the five changes is impossible — so nothing is stopping us.
steps.why: “Not one of them is impossible. That is the uncomfortable part.”

steps.title: Listen to one of three ideas on a radio programme.
steps.prompt: What is the idea?
options: One day a year when everybody gives a gift to a neighbour.
A new international sports day for every school in the world.
A tax on expensive presents so that people buy cheaper ones.
steps.answer: One day a year when everybody gives a gift to a neighbour.

steps.title: Listen to one of three ideas on a radio programme.
steps.prompt: What kind of gift does he suggest?
options: Something cheap but carefully chosen.
Something expensive and hard to find.
Money, so people can choose themselves.
steps.answer: Something cheap but carefully chosen.

steps.title: Listen to one of three ideas on a radio programme.
steps.prompt: What does he admit about his idea?
options: It wouldn’t solve the world’s serious problems.
It would cost far too much money to organize.
Nobody would take part in it after the first year.
steps.answer: It wouldn’t solve the world’s serious problems.

steps.title: Listen to the judge giving her opinion.
steps.sub: Notice how many second conditionals she uses.
steps.prompt: Would the judge take a smart pill?
options: Yes, if she knew it was safe.
No, she would never take one.
Only in exams, and nowhere else.
steps.answer: Yes, if she knew it was safe.

steps.title: Listen to the judge giving her opinion.
steps.sub: Notice how many second conditionals she uses.
steps.prompt: What is her worry?
options: The cost — only a few people could afford them.
The taste — most people would refuse to take them.
That they do not exist and probably never will.
steps.answer: The cost — only a few people could afford them.

steps.title: Listen to the judge on the other two ideas.
steps.prompt: What does the judge say about people who are not confident dancers?
options: If they danced a little every day, they would become confident.
They should not try to dance at all if they feel nervous.
They would need lessons from a teacher before they began.
steps.answer: If they danced a little every day, they would become confident.

steps.title: Listen to the judge on the other two ideas.
steps.prompt: What score does she give the last idea, and why?
options: 10 out of 10 — everybody can do it and it would make people happier.
8 out of 10 — it is a nice idea but it is far too much effort.
7 out of 10 — it is a good idea but it would be too expensive.
steps.answer: 10 out of 10 — everybody can do it and it would make people happier.
